claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy.
Lower-temperature phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is controlled by the kinetics of atomic ordering during cooling.
Slow cooling permits short-range ordering to develop in the BCC matrix.
Intermediate-temperature annealing permits short-range ordering to develop in the BCC matrix.
Short-range-order clusters act as nucleation sites or precursors for secondary-phase precipitation.
Formation of short-range order lowers the local free energy.
Slow cooling or moderate annealing provides sufficient atomic mobility for ordering and phase separation.
Rapid cooling suppresses diffusion and atomic ordering.
Rapid water quenching preserves Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 primarily as single-phase BCC with minimal short-range order.
Slowly cooled or annealed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will contain more detectable secondary phases than the water-quenched baseline.
The secondary phases produced by slow cooling or annealing may include FCC precipitates or intermetallic particles.
Slowly cooled or annealed samples will show greater compositional partitioning than water-quenched samples.
Cooling or annealing protocol will alter precipitate size, precipitate volume fraction, and chemical segregation.
The proposed mechanism operates only when the cooling rate or annealing duration allows sufficient atomic diffusion.
The proposed mechanism should not operate during extremely rapid cooling or thermal exposures too short to permit ordering.
APT or EDS mapping can verify the development of short-range order in these samples.
The exact cooling-rate thresholds and the composition and volume fraction of secondary phases are unknown.

A lack of any statistically significant difference in phase constitution, short-range order, or precipitation between quenched and slowly cooled or annealed samples would falsify the proposed mediation mechanism.
